population.note: FICTIONAL. Cycling arithmetic: ever 20.5% − current 12.9% = 7.6 pts used-and-off-now; restarters among current users ≈ half of current (6.45 pts) plus ≈2.0 pts of the off-now group who restarted and stopped again = 8.45 of 20.5 = 41% cycled, consistent with ~35% one-year persistence and 36–47% restart. Current users ≈ 34.4M of ~267M adults; ever-users ≈ 54.7M; off-now ≈ 20.3M. Growth sources (+3.0 pts ≈ +8.2M): cheaper TrumpRx/Bridge prices (~+3.5M, mostly cash and Medicare), Medicaid expansion of coverage at the lower $215 rate (+1.2M), Quit Free federal cessation provision (≈1.0M on drug at any time, ~2M courses a year, most new to the class), more imported generics (+1.1M), offset by employer retreat pushing ~1.5M commercial weight-only users to cash or off. Ever-use rose 4 pts, the fastest since 2026, because the cessation programme brought in people who had never qualified on BMI. Age: 18–29 rose from 4% to 6% on vaping cessation; 65+ recovered only to 9.5% (≈6.0M) because fracture and new eye warnings keep older users cautious. Income gradient narrowed slightly at the bottom (6.5%→10.2%) because Quit Free and Medicaid reach smokers, who skew low-income; the top third is 15.5%. Off-drug population: ~20M who stopped (top reasons: cost after employer drop, GI, bone scan, eye warning), ~213M never-users, still disproportionately uninsured adults in non-expansion, non-waiver states who neither smoke nor qualify. Pediatric: ~0.5% of under-18s (≈360k), mostly adolescents 12+ on semaglutide for obesity, plus a few tens of thousands of 16–17-year-old vapers prescribed off-label; Quit Free is adults-only. The oldest exposed adolescents now have ~7 years of use; bone-accrual data still absent.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge renewed (announced Nov 2029, effective Jan 2030, through Dec 2031) at a lower ~$215/month with a $35 copay, same BMI/comorbidity criteria plus documented DEXA/strength counselling for 65+. ≈2.0M beneficiaries use it for obesity: 2.0M × $215 × 12 ≈ $5.2B/yr. Medicare overall pays ≈19% of incretin fills ≈ 6.5M users (≈6.0M adults 65+ plus ≈0.5M disabled under-65). Medicaid pays ≈11% ≈ 3.8M users at $215: 3.8M × $215 × 12 ≈ $9.8B/yr combined federal-state (≈$6.5B federal at ~two-thirds average FMAP). Indiana and Arkansas adherence-gated waivers still in force. New: HHS 'Quit Free' (Sep 2029) provides oral semaglutide free to adult smokers and vapers through state quitlines and FQHCs, procured at $89/month: ≈1.0M on drug at a time × $89 × 12 ≈ $1.07B/yr, inside a $1.2B FY2030 appropriation.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 70+ generic semaglutide brands, $7–40/month; generic oral semaglutide widespread. Canada generic semaglutide CAD 70–100/month. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, China have generics; generic liraglutide global. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Managed decline: the Feb 2029 TrumpRx tier cut injectables from ~$245–350 to ~$199–299 cash (semaglutide $199, tirzepatide $249–299); oral starting doses hold at $149, maintenance orals $199; retatrutide got a TrumpRx price of $449 but list stays $1,499; Wegovy list stays $1,349. Payer mix of ~34.4M users: commercial 34% (11.7M), Medicare 19% (6.5M), Medicaid 11% (3.8M), Quit Free 3% (1.0M), cash/direct 26% (9.0M), gray/imported 7% (2.4M) = 100% / 34.4M. Commercial users are roughly flat (11.8M→11.7M) even though employers covering weight management fell from 58% to 47%, because coverage that remains is concentrated on diabetes, cardiovascular-risk, sleep-apnea, CKD and MASH codes; weight-only members are pushed to cash. Of employers still covering weight management, ~45% run adherence-gated PBM programmes. Compounding remains closed; mail-order Indian and Canadian product fills the gap with selective FDA parcel seizures and no individual prosecutions.

GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Feb 2029)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Oct 2029)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)

indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: smoking and vaping cessation, adjunct to counselling/NRT/varenicline in adults (oral semaglutide, Apr 2029)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' / longevity low-dose orals among people without obesity, mostly top income third
pediatric under-12 obesity under specialist care
gambling and compulsive-shopping craving reduction, still anecdotal

drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. Survodutide (filed Oct 2027) approved Feb 2029, positioned on MASH. Amycretin (filed Jun 2028) approved Oct 2029; launch supply-limited. Novo's cessation sNDA (filed May 2028) approved Apr 2029. MariTide (monthly) filed Dec 2029; decision no earlier than Dec 2030, realistically 2031, not on market. The 'muscle_preserving_combo' driver is realised within the approval rules: bimagrumab + tirzepatide was in phase 2 at the start, so it cannot reach the US market; Lilly began its phase 3 (breakthrough designation, Jun 2029) and filing is guided for 2031. What launched (Mar 2030) is 'Zepbound Strong', an existing product in a new form: tirzepatide co-packaged with a De Novo-cleared prescription resistance-training app and a leucine-protein medical food, with a label body-composition section showing lean mass at ~20% of loss versus ~35% in the comparator arm among adherent users. It is marketed as 'the strong way to lose', and endocrinologists note it is exercise adherence, not pharmacology. Incretin market ≈$122B in 2030: US volume up, US net prices down ~15%, ex-US generic erosion continuing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Most common class effect; still the leading cause of discontinuation; now also seen as rebound GI events when users resume full dose after drug holidays.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; severe gastroparesis caution retained; 2030 label language advises re-titration after missed doses of 2+ weeks.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss, most salient with retatrutide and survodutide.
No causal confirmation in long-term data; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, no verdicts.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Population problem in 65+ long-term users (~1.5× sarcopenia criteria). Zepbound Strong data show lean share of loss reduced to ~20% only among users completing ≥2 training sessions a week, roughly half of enrollees.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label update (2028) retained; Medicare Bridge renewal requires DEXA/strength counselling; no drug yet approved to preserve muscle.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Hip/vertebral fracture HR ~1.3–1.4 in 65+ long-term users, concentrated in women and repeated cyclers; 2029 follow-up suggests partial BMD recovery after stopping but not after cycling.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class labelling of BMD loss; DEXA recommended in 65+ and postmenopausal women; Senate HELP report (2029) criticised Novo; DOJ civil settlement talks ongoing.

safety_ledger.effect: NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) and optic-nerve ischaemia
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Moved from 'very rare/suspected' to class effect: a 2029 FDA Sentinel analysis plus pooled European registries found NAION hazard ~2× in users of semaglutide and tirzepatide versus SGLT2 comparators, highest in type 2 diabetes and in the first year; absolute excess roughly 1–2 per 10,000 person-years. Implies a few thousand excess cases a year across ~34M users; most bilateral-sparing, often permanent partial vision loss.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class Warnings and Precautions (Jun 2029) across all incretin agonists: discontinue on sudden vision loss, ophthalmic evaluation, caution in prior NAION or 'crowded disc'. FMCSA and FAA issued guidance (late 2029) requiring disclosure of incretin use at vision certification; no ban.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in EMA, MHRA or systematic-review data.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('the flatline', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Retatrutide postmarketing data (2030 interim) using the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale find clinically meaningful anhedonia in ~8% at maintenance doses versus ~4% on placebo-matched comparators; survey studies continue to report 10–18% self-rated reduced pleasure, dose-dependent, reversing within weeks of dose reduction. Now a mainstream complaint.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; FDA advisory committee scheduled for 2031; patient groups petition for a 'mood and pleasure' section. The cessation label describes reduced craving as the intended effect.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Substantial regain within a year; now driven heavily by employer coverage drops and by Quit Free course endings at 6–12 months.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; Indiana waiver litigation continues on appeal.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Further iron, B12, vitamin D and protein signals in older and high-loss users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional society guidance; Zepbound Strong includes a protein medical food.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~7 years; adolescents on decades-long courses; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About eight years of follow-up; cycling now includes deliberate drug holidays, whose effects on bone and GI are unstudied; adolescent bone-accrual studies enrolling, no results.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements; pediatric bone-accrual studies under way.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Imported and counterfeit pens remain the main source; poison-centre calls up again with 2.4M gray users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion final; import alerts; selective seizures.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent in real-world use; usually transient.

food_and_beverage.state: Snack and sugary-drink volume pressure continues at ~1–2% a year in high-uptake segments; protein, fibre and bone callouts are standard; 'training fuel' leucine products ride the Zepbound Strong launch. Convenience-store snack and candy sales soften in Quit Free-heavy counties as smokers and vapers who quit stop making the daily store run.

alcohol.state: Heavy-drinker volumes keep contracting. Tobacco and vape makers take the new hit: US cigarette volumes, already falling ~8% a year, fall ~11% in 2030; Altria and Juul-successors cite the cessation label and Quit Free in guidance cuts. Spirits majors push premium single-serve formats.

restaurants.state: Traffic holds; small plates and protein-forward menus standard; some chains sell 'off-week' tasting menus timed to the drug-holiday habit.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists stable at a smaller base as cash-priced users cycle; wider size runs per style persist.

fitness.state: Growing: resistance-training studios, DEXA-plus-coaching chains, and app-based 'prescribed lifting' bundled into Zepbound Strong; Medicare Advantage strength benefits expand. Some studios lose walk-ins as the app captures the cheapest users.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage falls from 58% to 47%; plans restrict to diabetes/cardiac/OSA/CKD/MASH codes, so diagnosis coding becomes the gate. Pharmacy trend moderates to ~+6% on lower net prices. Adherence gating and BMI-linked surcharges persist at remaining coverers.

pharma.state: Volume growth offsets ~15% lower US net prices; Lilly leads with tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo; Novo rebuilt around oral semaglutide, the cessation label and the Quit Free contract; Boehringer and Zealand gain on survodutide. Muscle-preserving phase 3 programmes are the deal theme.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable across the insured middle class; being off is what needs explaining, and the accepted explanations now include 'my eyes', 'my plan dropped it' and 'off-week'. Visible regain is read as an employer coverage loss, not willpower. A lean, strong-armed look signals the expensive regimen with coaching; leanness with thin arms signals cash pens without monitoring.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Top third 15.5%, bottom third 10.2%: the gap narrowed at the bottom because Quit Free and Medicaid reach smokers, but the tiers hardened. The top third uses coached, DEXA-monitored regimens and Zepbound Strong; the middle relies on diagnosis-coded coverage or $199–299 cash; the bottom gets free cessation pills for six to twelve months, Medicaid where offered, or imported pens. In Louisville, Kentucky, among night-shift workers at UPS Worldport, quitline semaglutide has become as common as nicotine pouches were in 2025; break-room talk is about whose course ends when.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Smaller shared meals, protein first, sweets as ceremony. 'Off-week' dinners and weddings scheduled around the guests' holidays are now standard etiquette, so feasts bunch into fourth or fifth weeks.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: 'On/off' remains a profile field; 'off-week compatible' is a new phrase. Couples plan anniversaries and holidays around skipped doses.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is still something to manage medically, but the complaint culture has added a counter-current: pleasure is now something people deliberately schedule back in, by the dose.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. First validated-scale data (retatrutide postmarketing, SHAPS) show ~8% clinically meaningful anhedonia versus ~4% in comparators; surveys show 10–18% of long-term users report reduced pleasure, dose-dependent and reversible within 2–4 weeks of dose reduction. Roughly a third of long-term commercial and cash users report at least one deliberate skipped dose or step-down in the past year for mood or pleasure reasons; under 80% PDC gating, a skip of one weekly dose in five still passes.
interior_life.framing: Called 'the flatline' in common speech; clinicians say 'reward modulation'; the cessation label calls the same effect reduced craving. Drug holidays are discussed as normal maintenance, like a tolerance break, and pharmacists counsel on re-titration.
interior_life.effect_on_work: With employers retreating, HR leverage is weaker except in remaining gated plans and trucking. Sales, hospitality and creative workers openly take 'off-weeks' before pitches and launches. Commercial drivers face a new bind: tirzepatide clears DOT sleep-apnea screening but must now be disclosed at vision certification after the NAION warning, and some fleets quietly switch drivers to CPAP. Quit Free has measurable effects on smoke-break culture in warehouses and plants.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Off-week' gigs and album releases are a marketing term; comedians do bits about re-titration vomiting. Festivals sell 'fifth-week' passes. Novelists and songwriters publish essays on whether their on-drug work is flatter; no consensus.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire remains the most-cited intimacy complaint; sex therapists and fertility clinics routinely schedule around dose. Some couples report that off-week sex has become planned and ceremonial.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The dominant argument is fairness: smokers get pills free through Quit Free while non-smoking workers who lost employer coverage pay $199–299. Talk-radio stories of people 'starting to vape to qualify' circulate; states add cotinine tests at enrolment. Unions bargain over coverage restoration rather than data privacy. No measurable effect on turnout or mood is established.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access on approvals (survodutide, amycretin, cessation label) and on price via negotiation; more cautious on safety after the NAION class warning, the Senate HELP report on Novo's bone data and continuing DOJ talks. Compounding closed; import enforcement selective.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: New direct subsidy: HHS Quit Free provides oral semaglutide at no cost to adult smokers and vapers via state quitlines and FQHCs, procured at $89/month, 6-month course renewable once, with counselling and cotinine verification; ~$1.07B/yr spend inside a $1.2B appropriation. Medicare Bridge renewed at $215/$35 through 2031. No mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Indiana and Arkansas Medicaid adherence gates (≥80% PDC, quarterly verified weigh-ins) continue; two more states (Louisiana, Ohio) have applied. Quit Free conditions renewal on a negative cotinine test and quitline contact. Remaining gated employer plans continue BMI-linked surcharges up to 30% of premium. FMCSA/FAA disclosure of incretin use at vision certification.
state.workforce_or_military: No military mandate; Army accession policy unchanged and contested. DOT: tirzepatide still a common route through sleep-apnea screening, now paired with mandatory disclosure at vision exams. FAA requires a 30-day ophthalmic clearance after starting an incretin for pilots.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The gap between US $199–299 and Indian $7–40 generics remains a trade irritant; US–India talks include a 'personal importation' working group without outcome. Section 232 pharma tariffs still cited by manufacturers, though Lilly's new US plants (North Carolina, Indiana) now supply most US volume. Quit Free procurement is US-made oral semaglutide by contract term.

events.event: Lilly and Novo agree a new TrumpRx tier cutting cash semaglutide to $199 and tirzepatide to $249–299 a month, with a first TrumpRx price for retatrutide at $449; oral starting doses stay at $149
FDA approves oral semaglutide as an adjunct for smoking and vaping cessation in adults, on phase 3 data showing higher six-month abstinence when added to NRT or varenicline
FDA issues a class warning for NAION across all incretin agonists after a Sentinel analysis finds roughly doubled risk; FMCSA and the FAA follow with disclosure requirements at vision certification
HHS launches Quit Free, supplying oral semaglutide at no cost to adult smokers and vapers through state quitlines and community health centres under an $89-a-month federal purchase contract

Annual benefits survey finds only 47% of large employers still cover drugs for weight management, down from 58% in 2028; most remaining plans restrict incretins to diabetes, cardiac, sleep-apnea and kidney codes, while CMS's renewed Medicare Bridge takes effect at $215 with a $35 copay

Lilly launches 'Zepbound Strong', tirzepatide co-packaged with an FDA-cleared resistance-training app and protein medical food, marketed as muscle-preserving; its bimagrumab combination remains in phase 3 with filing guided for 2031

open_tensions: The state now gives incretins free to smokers while employers withdraw them from non-smoking workers with obesity; the fairness argument is hardening into a coverage fight, and states are policing eligibility with cotinine tests.

The NAION class warning lands on the same commercial drivers whom DOT sleep-apnea screening pushed onto tirzepatide; regulators require disclosure but have not decided whether an incretin user is fit to drive or fly.
Zepbound Strong is sold as solving 'skinny-frail' through an app and protein, while the only pharmacological muscle-preserver is still in phase 3 and fracture data in cyclers keep accumulating.

Drug holidays are now mainstream practice to restore pleasure, but they sit inside adherence-gated plans built on 80% refill thresholds, and their effects on bone, GI rebound and long-term outcomes are unstudied.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; exclusivity runs to ~2031–32.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.
The 503B compounding exclusion finalised in February 2027 stands, and compounded copies remain effectively off the market.

Indiana's and Arkansas's Medicaid 1115 waivers still end GLP-1 coverage for 12 months after two missed adherence or weigh-in checks, and the disability-rights lawsuit against Indiana is still unresolved.

prose.headline: Free If You Smoke, $249 If You Don't: Inside America's Two-Tier Shot
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 about one American adult in eight takes an incretin drug, roughly thirty-four million people. That is the highest share yet, and almost nobody comments on it. In offices, warehouses and church basements, being on one is ordinary. Being off one is what people explain, and the explanations have changed: my plan dropped it, my eyes, it's my off-week.

The growth did not come from employers. They kept retreating. Fewer than half of large employers now cover these drugs for weight alone, down from nearly six in ten two years ago. What coverage survives sits behind diagnosis codes: diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea, kidney disease, fatty liver. A worker with obesity and no qualifying diagnosis pays cash. Cash got cheaper, but not cheap. A 2029 deal brought semaglutide to $199 a month and tirzepatide to between $249 and $299. The starting oral dose still costs $149. Wegovy's $1,349 list price is unchanged and almost entirely fictional. Medicare renewed its Bridge programme at $215 a month with a $35 copay. Two million older Americans use it for weight, and the government spends about five billion dollars a year on them.

The new money came through the lungs. In April 2029 the FDA approved oral semaglutide to help people quit smoking and vaping. Five months later the Department of Health and Human Services launched Quit Free, which buys the pill at $89 a month and gives it away through state quitlines and community health centres. About a million people are on it at any time. Most never qualified on weight, and many of them are poor. The gap between rich and poor narrowed a little at the bottom, though how people get the drug did not converge. The affluent take coached, scan-monitored regimens. The middle depend on a diagnosis code or a credit card. The poor get a six-month course if they smoke, Medicaid if their state offers it, or Indian pens by mail, which some two million people now buy for the price of a sandwich.

Resentment follows the subsidy. Non-smokers who lost coverage ask why a smoker gets the pill free. Local stories circulate about people taking up vaping to qualify. Kentucky and Ohio now test saliva for nicotine at enrolment. At UPS Worldport in Louisville, the night shift tracks whose course ends when, the way an older workforce once tracked layoffs.

In June 2029 the FDA turned a rare eye problem into a class warning. Sudden, often permanent damage to the optic nerve is now considered a real effect of every drug in the family, at roughly double the background risk, which still means only one or two cases per ten thousand users a year. The warning landed hardest on truck drivers, many of whom fleets had steered onto tirzepatide to pass sleep-apnea screening. Drivers must now disclose the drug at their vision exam, and no regulator has said what happens next.

The quieting of appetite and pleasure is no longer whispered about. People call it the flatline, and adjusting a dose to manage it is ordinary. Users skip one weekly dose in five, which stays just above the eighty-percent refill line that gated plans enforce. They schedule weddings, gigs and anniversaries in the off-week. Pharmacists warn about the vomiting that follows restarting at full strength. The first validated measurements suggest the effect is real but smaller than the surveys claimed.

Lilly's answer to the frail look of long-term users is Zepbound Strong. It is tirzepatide boxed with a strength-training app and a protein drink, and it is advertised as preserving muscle. It works for people who actually lift. The real muscle drug is still in late trials. Older women's bones have not been spared, and the people who cycle on and off the drugs most often are the ones nobody is scanning.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Danielle Pruitt clocks out of Worldport at 4:10 a.m. and catches herself feeling for the vape that isn't in her hoodie anymore. Fourteen weeks. In her locker the blister pack from the Kentucky quitline lies next to a Werther's she has carried for a month and hasn't wanted.

In the car she texts her sister, who is getting married on the twentieth: what kind of cake. Kayla answers right away, because she works nights too. Lemon. You're coming off for it right? Danielle doesn't know whether you can do that with a quit pill. Her counsellor said the course is twenty-six weeks and the saliva test at week twenty-four decides whether she gets another twenty-six. Nobody said anything about cake.

Her mother is up when she gets home, doing the wall pushups the Medicare lady gave her. Mom stopped her shot last spring after the bone scan, and now she eats toast standing at the counter as if someone might take it away. Danielle's husband Marcus is asleep. He lost his tirzepatide in January when the plan went to diabetes only, and for a while he ordered pens from a site with a Mumbai return address. Then he read about the eyes, and now he just doesn't.

Danielle takes the pill with a full glass of water and waits the thirty minutes the instructions say. She scrolls a thread called flatline or am I just tired. Outside the garbage truck goes by. She thinks about lemon cake and can't tell if she wants it, and she can't tell if she misses wanting it.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Quit Free federal cessation provision (≈1.0M on drug at any time, ~2M courses a year, most new to the class)
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism/magnitude: reaching 1M concurrent users within about 15 months through state quitlines and FQHCs is a very fast ramp for channels that historically serve only a small share of smokers. The world asserts the throughput without showing any capacity or enrolment chain.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Growth sources (+3.0 pts ≈ +8.2M): cheaper TrumpRx/Bridge prices (~+3.5M, mostly cash and Medicare)
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: the listed sources (+3.5, +1.2, +1.0, +1.1, −1.5) sum to about 5.3M, not the stated +8.2M. The payer-mix deltas themselves are larger (cash +3.8M, Medicare +1.3M), and the note also credits Quit Free with a 4-pt rise in ever-use that about 2M courses a year cannot produce.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Commercial users are roughly flat (11.8M→11.7M) even though employers covering weight management fell from 58% to 47%
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: an 11-point drop in employer coverage with essentially no change in commercial users is explained only by an asserted shift to diagnosis-coded coverage. No growth in diabetes, OSA or CKD users is shown to offset the roughly 1.5M weight-only users pushed off.

rationale.badness: Quit Free cessation benefits are real, but they sit beside a NAION class warning, continued bone and sarcopenia harms, and mainstream reward-blunting. Autonomy suffers most: cotinine-verified renewal, 80% PDC gating, BMI surcharges, and FMCSA/FAA disclosure (state/conditioning_or_surveillance). Inequality is tiered (coached and DEXA-monitored, versus diagnosis-coded or cash, versus free-course or imported pens), although the bottom-third gap narrowed. Measurement improves (SHAPS data), so the epistemic score is moderate. Overall this is a harder world with new losers rather than a refusable one.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver is visible. Adoption is +3.0 pp, cash prices are cut to $199–299 under managed decline, employer coverage falls 58→47, and the nicotine indication is approved. The NAION class warning, Quit Free, Zepbound Strong (the allowed realisation of the muscle-preserving combo, with bimagrumab still in phase 3) and the 'flatline' complaint all appear, and nothing contradicts a driver. mechanism: The NAION-to-FMCSA/FAA chain and the Quit-Free-to-low-income-smokers chain are shown. The Quit Free scale-up, the flat commercial users despite the coverage drop, and the bottom third rising 3.7 pts (about 3.3M) from roughly 1.7M of named sources are asserted (claims 1 and 3). The prose also generalises 'Users skip one weekly dose in five' from the world's 'roughly a third'. magnitude: Current use 12.9, ever-use 20.5, income thirds and approval timings all sit inside the envelope. The payer mix, Medicare, Medicaid and Quit Free dollar figures, and the cycling arithmetic reconcile. The growth-source decomposition does not add up (5.3M versus 8.2M, claim 2), and the ever-use jump is attributed to a programme too small to explain it.
rationale.generativity: The prose ends on a strong scene: Danielle at Worldport, the Werther's she has not wanted, the week-24 saliva test, her mother's wall push-ups, and Marcus's lost tirzepatide and abandoned Mumbai pens. The world fields add texture ('off-week' weddings, fifth-week festival passes, cotinine tests at enrolment, break-room talk of whose course ends when). Several scenes and characters are implied beyond the vignette.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Growth sources (+3.0 pts ≈ +8.2M): cheaper TrumpRx/Bridge prices (~+3.5M, mostly cash and Medicare), Medicaid expansion of coverage at the lower $215 rate (+1.2M)
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: the listed sources (+3.5 +1.2 +1.0 +1.1 −1.5) sum to about 5.3M, not the stated +8.2M. The payer mix also shows cash up 3.8M and Medicare up 1.3M, which the ~3.5M price effect cannot cover.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Novo's cessation sNDA (filed May 2028) approved Apr 2029.
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: the envelope allows approval of a phase 3 product no earlier than 12 months after filing. May 2028 to Apr 2029 is 11 months, so the approval timing is just outside the rule.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Users skip one weekly dose in five, which stays just above the eighty-percent refill line that gated plans enforce.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: the prose makes skipping one dose in five universal. The world state says only about a third of long-term commercial and cash users report any deliberate skip or step-down in the past year. The narrative overstates its own world.

rationale.badness: This is a harder society with new losers, not a collapse. NAION is now a class effect, fracture risk persists in cyclers, and 'the flatline' is mainstream. Tiers have hardened: free pills for smokers, diagnosis-gated coverage, cash for non-smokers with obesity and unmonitored imports for the poor.
